findings.explanation: AES-256-GCM is used correctly as an algorithm, but every encryption call reuses the same fixed, all-zero 12-byte IV (line 32-33) with the same derived key instead of generating a fresh random IV per call. GCM security depends on IV uniqueness per key: reusing it lets an attacker XOR two ciphertexts to cancel the keystream and recover plaintext relationships, and once the keystream for one IV is known, forge valid GCM auth tags for other messages under the same key. This is functionally equivalent to using a broken cipher mode even though the primitive itself (AES-256-GCM) is strong. Fix: crypto.randomBytes(12) per call, store the IV alongside the ciphertext (the format already has an ivPart field so this is a low-effort fix).

The AES-256-GCM key is derived from the master key by a single raw SHA-256 hash rather than a proper KDF (HKDF/PBKDF2/scrypt). A raw hash provides no key-stretching and is not designed as a KDF, so if CREDENTIAL_MASTER_KEY is ever a lower-entropy value (not a truly random 256-bit secret), the derived key inherits that weakness. Not urgent since the master key is presumably a strong generated secret, but should use crypto.hkdfSync or similar for defense in depth.
